description: Hello! We’re two sisters with an insatiable thirst for knowledge. We both come from marketing, operations and tech, so we know how to build something, keep it on track, and explain it so people care. We want to build a tool that lets you pick Earth-science data and find out what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is real or just noise. It’s made for students and other curious souls.
summary:
"Summers feel hotter than when I was young." 

Claims like this spread much faster than anyone can check them. Thy Will Be Done lets a student, a teacher or a local journalist check one in about a minute, using NASA data, and get an honest answer in plain words: 

real /possible /or not proven yet.

You type a question ("Is the Earth spinning faster?", "Are summers getting hotter?"):

1. The app picks the right NASA variable and explains what it measures. 
2. You choose a place and years, and lock in your own prediction before seeing anything. 
3. Then it shows the record and tests the trend the way scientists do. 
4. The answer is one sentence, backed by a 7-point "Is it real?" checklist and a one-page report you can share.

Worked example, our own city:
Are summers in Beirut getting hotter? Yes. 

The hottest summer days have warmed by about 0.35 °C per decade since 1981, roughly 1.6 °C in 45 years. Two different tests agree (p < 0.01), with the seasonal cycle and year-to-year memory accounted for (NASA POWER, MERRA-2).

Why you can trust it: 
We ran the same tests on six questions where science already knows the answer. 
The tool gets five right, and we show the one it misses and why. 

Bonus: It works in English, Arabic and French.
details:
What it does:

Thy Will Be Done turns the challenge's five steps into a guided "Detective":

  1. Choose a variable. Type a question in everyday words (English, Arabic or French) or browse a topic. Each variable comes with a plain definition and why a trend in it would matter.
  2. Choose a place. The whole world, a continent, a desert, a rainforest, an estuary, an ocean, a country or the air above a big city. The app suggests what detectives usually check in that kind of place.
  3. Choose the years and season. Some trends only show in summer or winter.
  4. Predict, then look. You lock a prediction (rising, falling or no clear trend) before the chart appears, then make your own call.
  5. Test it. The app gives the rate of change per decade with a confidence range, two significance tests (Mann-Kendall and a t-test), and a plain-language verdict. When a trend is not significant yet, the checklist estimates how many years of data a trend that size would need.

Is it real? Seven checks on every result:

  1. the seasonal cycle was removed;
  2. memory in the data (autocorrelation) was allowed for;
  3. two different tests agree;
  4. the answer does not hinge on one or two odd years;
  5. it does not depend on the start year;
  6. it runs in the same direction in both halves of the record;
  7. the record is long enough.

Every investigation can be downloaded as a one-page report.

Beyond one trend

  • My place. Tests every NASA POWER variable at any city or coordinates in about 10 seconds and lists the changes in plain sentences.
    • Checks whether two things are linked, against surrogates that keep each series' own rhythm.
    • Checks whether a result holds up in other regions and in held-back years.
    • Checks whether events cluster at one time of year.
    • Checks whether events follow extreme conditions.
  • Known answers. The same tests run on six questions with established answers. The tool gets five right. It calls the slow weakening of Earth's magnetic field "not proven", because smooth model data leaves too few independent values. We show this miss rather than hide it.
  • Seraph, a guide. A small angel mascot explains what each section does.
  • Two demos. Real investigations to watch step by step: wildfire smoke from Wisconsin to Canada, and haze trending in opposite directions over India and China (the same process, opposite trends in two regions).

How it addresses the challenge

The challenge asks for a tool that:

  • selects mission or model variables;
  • visualizes change over time for a region;
  • runs a basic significance test;
  • serves high-school and college students and the public, with simple definitions, a short series of questions and demonstration examples.

Thy Will Be Done does all of this. It also handles the pitfalls the challenge mentions: it removes seasonal cycles, explains that a non-significant trend may only need a longer record, and suggests variables based on the kind of region.

What we found with it (full results: https://claude.ai/artifact/NLb2pxctabeDLkqqoNrkY1 < take a look!)

  • Earth's days are getting shorter. Since 1962, the length of day has dropped by about 0.44 milliseconds per decade (p = 0.0003), and the shortest day on record was 5 July 2024. The checklist flags that the answer depends on the start year, because the swings are decades long.
  • Summer haze is rising in central Canada, near the recent large wildfires. Over Wisconsin, downwind, it is only possibly rising.
  • Large earthquakes show no long-term trend, and the apparent rise in recorded volcanic eruptions disappears once better reporting after 1960 is accounted for.
  • The tool finds the Sun's known grip on geomagnetic activity, but no replicable link between solar activity, magnetic storms or seasonal water loads and earthquakes.

How we built it

  • The app is written in Python with Streamlit, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels and Plotly.
  • Trend test. A modified Mann-Kendall test (Hamed and Rao 1998) with Sen's slope, plus a least-squares t-test with the same autocorrelation allowance. A change counts as real only when both agree.
  • Many tests at once. A false-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) when many variables are tested together.
  • Links. Phase-randomised surrogates for links, and shift tests for event timing.
  • Data. Plug-in "connectors" add each source; the app also recognises files exported from NASA Giovanni, NASA AppEEARS, NOAA Climate Data Online and the KNMI Climate Explorer.
  • Tests. 84 automated tests cover the statistics, the parsers and the translations.

References

Methods

  • Hamed, K. H. and Rao, A. R. (1998), A modified Mann-Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data, Journal of Hydrology 204, 182–196.
  • Sen, P. K. (1968), Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau, JASA 63, 1379–1389.
  • Benjamini, Y. and Hochberg, Y. (1995), Controlling the false discovery rate, JRSS B 57, 289–300.
  • Theiler, J. et al. (1992), Testing for nonlinearity in time series: the method of surrogate data, Physica D 58, 77–94.
  • Challenge resource: "Time-Series Analysis of Remotely-Sensed SeaWiFS Chlorophyll in River-Influenced Coastal Regions" (NASA NTRS 20090042747).

Software
Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, xarray, Plotly, earthaccess and Playwright (for recording the demo videos).
